articles.title: Lo nuevo de Instagram recorta y edita tus Reels con un toque y sin IA
articles.text:
Si editas tus Reels en el móvil, sabrás lo tedioso que puede llegar a ser. Dependiendo de tu nivel de "influencer", el proceso puede ir desde un simple ajuste en la app de Instagram o CapCut hasta otra herramienta externa. Meta ha decidido simplificar el proceso con First Draft (o primer borrador), una nueva función que ya está disponible en la app de Instagram.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su cuenta de Threads, First Draft puede cortar pausas y recortar los clips de forma automática con un solo toque. La herramienta analiza los vídeos que seleccionas y elimina los silencios para quedarte con lo más relevante. El resultado es un primer borrador del Reel, listo para que lo ajustes a tu gusto o lo publiques al momento.
Para usarlo solo necesitas grabar o seleccionar tus clips en la galería de Reels, tocar el botón de First Draft y esperar que la app haga el resto en cuestión de segundos. En caso de que tengas varios clips de más de un minuto cada uno, Instagram los analiza y detecta las partes con pausas largas o momentos muertos para descartarlos del corte final. Después de eso, la herramienta une los fragmentos seleccionados en un solo vídeo y permite una edición más a detalle, como reordenar escenas, eliminar partes o ajustar la duración.
También es posible empezar de cero si el resultado no te convence, ya que todos los cambios de First Draft se guardan en un borrador completamente editable. Esta herramienta funciona bien con distintos tipos de contenido, como montajes, vídeos tipo talking-head o publicaciones de día a día. El objetivo es ahorrarte el trabajo de recortar clip por clip para concentrarte en la parte creativa.
Instagram no usa IA en su nueva función First Draft
Por increíble que parezca, la nueva función de Instagram no utiliza inteligencia artificial. Esto es difícil de creer, sobre todo si consideramos que Meta está invirtiendo una cantidad indiscriminable de dinero para impulsar sus modelos en Meta AI. Sin embargo, este no es el caso, al menos en First Draft.
Nicole Rechtszaid, responsable de comunicación de Instagram, confirmó a The Verge que su sistema se basa en detección de pausas y silencios. A diferencia de Quick Cut de Adobe, que combina clips mediante indicaciones basadas en IA, la herramienta de Instagram opta por algo más tradicional. La compañía prefiere ocupar esos recursos de cómputo en otras funciones más indispensables dentro de sus otras aplicaciones.
Si quieres usar First Draft para crear tu primer borrador, solo necesitas abrir la cámara de Instagram y grabar tu vídeo (o seleccionar los clips). Posteriormente, basta tocar el botón ubicado en la parte inferior para esperar que IG haga su magia. Lamentablemente, esta función solo está disponible para iPhone y no se ha confirmado si llegará a Android en un futuro cercano.

articles.title: Your vote matters! Decide which Audience Choice sessions will make it to TechCrunch Founder Summit | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Each year, we get a huge influx of applicants to speak at TechCrunch’s events, and this year’s Founder Summit in Boston on November 4 will be no different! We want to thank everyone who applied to take part in our programming and to help share their expertise with the startup community.
After careful review, we have 11 finalists who are vying for four slots within this year’s event agenda, and each one showcases the kind of practical, essential insights that can only be delivered by those who have built, iterated, and succeeded.
You can vote via this link to weigh in on which sessions ultimately make the cut. Submissions will close on September 4. If you’re voting and haven’t already gotten your Founder Summit tickets this year, what are you waiting for?
On November 4 in Boston, you’ll get the chance to learn directly from the experts in intimate, exclusive sessions that can put you ahead of the competition or set you up to play a pivotal role in developing the next era of innovators. We still have discounts running on tickets that can save you up to $100 right here!
With that said, let’s dive into our Disrupt Audience Choice nominees, and remember: The voting takes place via this form, so take a look and then submit your vote!
How to Build Events Strategy Before You Can Afford a Full-Time Events Team
Alexandra Ames: Founder and Chief Event Strategist, Blueprint Lab
Early-stage founders approach events one of two ways: say yes to every opportunity, or avoid them entirely because the ROI feels impossible to justify. Neither is smart. Events can build your audience and credibility before product-market fit but only if you’re strategic about which ones deserve your time and budget. We’ll discuss how to think strategically when resources are tight, including how to maximize ROI from founder events like this one. You’ll leave with frameworks for prioritizing stage-appropriate event investments, tactics for proving value without complex tools, and clarity on when events make sense and when they don’t.
How to Build a “Made in the USA” Hardware Company and Actually Scale It
Hannan Happi: CEO and Co-Founder, Exowatt
Domestic manufacturing is back in the spotlight, but building hardware in the U.S. is still widely seen as too expensive to scale. This session explores how founders can design hardware companies that make “Made in the USA” economically viable from day one. We’ll break down supply chain strategy, cost structure, factory partnerships, and how policy tailwinds like the IRA and CHIPS Act change the equation. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for evaluating when domestic manufacturing can become a competitive advantage — not just a branding decision.
Build Something We Don’t Have a Word for Yet
Andy Tang: Partner, Draper Associates
Pitches that change industries rarely fit existing categories — and most investors will pass on them for exactly that reason. This talk explores why the most fundable startups are often the hardest ones to describe, and what that means for how you build and position yours. Founders will leave with a clearer sense of the difference between a market insight and a market-creating idea, and what it actually takes to get a pattern-matching investor to bet on something genuinely new — before the rest of the world has a name for it.
GraphRAG in Action: Stop Hallucinations with Knowledge Graphs
Shishir Tewari: Head of Enterprise Data Engineering, Procore Technologies
Are messy data sources causing your LLMs to hallucinate? Relational databases struggle to bridge the semantic gap for AI. Learn to build a production-ready GraphRAG pipeline that turns chaotic data into actionable insights. Actionable takeaways: Build an offline pipeline to resolve disjointed datasets into “golden records.” Translate flat records into an interconnected Neo4j knowledge graph. Deploy a secure, local LLM (Ollama) to translate natural language into validated Cypher queries. Give your AI the foundational data structure it needs!
The Enterprise AI Playbook: How to Close L’Oreal and Vodafone Before You Raise a Series A
Merve Kitapci: Managing Partner and CGO, ADIN.AI
Most founders chase product-market fit before landing enterprise clients. We did the opposite. This roundtable covers the exact motion for closing global enterprise accounts at pre-Series A: how to structure the first conversation with a Fortune 500 CMO; why agency partnerships accelerate enterprise sales; how to price with no brand recognition; and what zero organic churn means for your fundraising story. Attendees leave with a repeatable enterprise sales framework, an early-stage AI pricing model, and the three things that make a CMO say yes before legal sees the contract.
Lessons from 20 Years of Bootstrapping an Open Source Business to $50M+
Peter Farkas: CEO, Percona
Building a successful open source company without venture capital is rare — scaling it past $50 million in revenue is even rarer. This talk shares two decades of lessons from growing a commercial open source business from zero to global scale. We’ll cover product-market fit, monetizing open source while keeping the core free, building distributed teams before remote work was mainstream, and creating a repeatable go-to-market engine without outside funding. We’ll also discuss failures, hard lessons, and how to compete against well-funded alternatives while staying bootstrapped. Attendees will leave with practical strategies for scaling sustainably.
Small but Mighty: How AI Lets Lean Teams Outship the Giants
Linden Tibbets: CEO and Co-Founder, IFTTT
The playbook has flipped, and we have lived it firsthand. A five-person team can now outbuild, outship, and outmaneuver companies with 500 engineers. This roundtable gets into the tactical reality of running a lean, AI-powered team: which tools are actually worth your time, how to build workflows that compound instead of bloat, and where most teams are burning cycles on AI that goes nowhere. Walk away knowing how to audit your current stack for speed gaps, which AI-driven growth motions are converting right now, and how to use your small size as an advantage, not an excuse.
The Demo Trap: Why Impressive AI Doesn’t Always Build Real Companies
Jeff Mahler: Co-Founder and CTO, Ambi Robotics
In today’s AI boom, impressive demos can generate headlines, funding, and early excitement, but they rarely prove a real business by themselves. This session explores the gap between prototype performance and real-world deployment, and why many promising AI startups stall before reaching scale. Founders and investors will learn how to evaluate whether AI systems are truly ready for production, the operational and reliability metrics that matter most, and how to build companies that can move beyond hype to durable, real-world impact.
From CentOS to Rocky Linux: Building Movements That Outlast You
Gregory Kurtzer: CEO and Founder, CIQ
Greg Kurtzer helped create CentOS, one of the world’s most widely used operating systems, then founded CIQ and launched Rocky Linux when Red Hat discontinued CentOS. In this session, he shares hard-won lessons from building open source movements and a startup from scratch: why founders must leave ego at the door, then navigate the transition from hiring versatile generalists early, then moving to a team of specialists as you scale. He explains the mistake he almost made by dismissing the value of culture and core values, and what it really takes to build something durable.
The Healthcare AI Companies That Will Actually Matter
Vikram Chaudhery, PhD: CEO and Founder, Genoa Ventures
Most AI healthcare demos look incredible and ship nothing. The companies that will matter in 2026 aren’t the ones with the best models. They’re the ones that get decisions to clinicians in an actionable window and change what doctors actually do for the patient in real clinical workflows. This roundtable digs into what separates investable healthcare AI from expensive science fairs, where agentic systems are creating real value beyond copilots, what founders consistently get wrong before their Series A, and the bar that anyone funding, founding, or joining a healthcare AI company should apply.
How Technical AI Founders Get Into YC, a16z Speedrun, and Raise from Top-Tier VCs
George Bandarian: Founder and General Partner, Untapped Ventures
The best technical founders building in AI and robotics aren’t failing because of their product — they’re failing because they don’t understand what top investors are actually looking for. In this roundtable, early-stage technical founders will work through what YC, a16z speedrun, and top-tier VCs evaluate beyond the deck: founder-market fit signals, why most technical founders need a business counterpart earlier than they think, how to position an autonomous economy company for a lead investor, and what the fundraising process actually looks like before you have traction.

articles.title: Complete Farmer CEO Desmond Koney joins Endeavor Nigeria network - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Endeavor Nigeria has announced the selection of Desmond Koney, founder and CEO of Ghanaian agri-tech startup Complete Farmer, into its network, following a multi-stage selection process culminating at Endeavor’s International Selection Panel in Athens, Greece.
Complete Farmer is an agricultural trading company connecting international commodity buyers with smallholder farmers across Ghana and Togo. The company works with more than 72,000 farmers and supplies international buyers, including Aldi and Lidl, and its operations are supported by more than 350 field agents and eight fulfillment centres responsible for aggregation, grading, quality control and export logistics.
The startup has expanded beyond agricultural trading, developing a marketplace for farm inputs and equipment and a credit product that uses farm data to help farmers access financing. CEO Koney was selected for the Endeavor network alongside 27 other entrepreneurs leading 16 companies from markets across Europe, Africa, Asia, the Middle East and the Americas.
Joining Endeavor represents an opportunity to build beyond the company and contribute to Ghana’s broader entrepreneurial ecosystem.
“As the first Ghanaian company to join the Endeavor network, I also see this as something bigger than Complete Farmer. It creates a bridge between Ghana’s entrepreneurial ecosystem and a global community of founders, investors and business leaders. With that opportunity comes a responsibility to open doors for others, share what we learn and help more Ghanaian entrepreneurs access the relationships and resources that can support their own growth,” Koney said.
Ireayomide Oladunjoye, managing director of Endeavor Nigeria, said Koney was building a Ghanaian company with a distinctly regional and global opportunity.
His journey reflects the kind of entrepreneurship we believe can create meaningful economic impact while opening up new possibilities for the people and communities it serves. Welcoming Desmond into the Endeavor network is also an important opportunity to strengthen the connections between entrepreneurs across West Africa and the broader global network,” she said.

articles.title: Apple unveils powerhouse Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro and Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple has announced its latest powerhouse Mac computers with a new level of on-device AI – the Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro chips along with the new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Apple silicon.
They are available to pre-order today and will go on sale on September 22.
MAC MINI WITH M6 AND M5 PRO – From $1,449 (M6) and $2,699 (M5 Pro)
Mac mini with M6 offers 4x faster AI performance while the new Mac mini with M5 Pro can easily take on demanding assignments from video editing and production to game development.
And with this level of performance the new Mac mini could easily handle business workflows and be used as a primary desktop or powerful always-on desk-side agentic computer.
Mac mini with M6 has a 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest single-threaded performance to make everything feel faster and responsive.
It has a 12-core GPU. That’s two more cores than before and now includes neural accelerators in each core for the first time on Mac Mini.
The result is up to 4x faster performance with AI and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4.
Both Mac mini models have Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 plus upgraded 2.5Gb. Ethernet with a 10Gb option also available.
Mac mini with M6 delivers:
– Up to 13.5x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac mini with M1, and up to 4.8x faster than M4.
– Up to 2.3x faster spreadsheet calculations in Microsoft Excel when compared to Mac mini with M1, and up to 1.5x faster than M4.
– Up to 2x faster gaming performance with ray tracing in Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition when compared to Mac mini with M4.
The Mac Mini with M5 Pro will give customers a whole new appreciation for what’s possible with a small desktop computer.
We can take on demanding tasks like app development, video rendering, scientific simulations and much more.
M5 Pro has an 18-core CPU for next-level multi-threaded performance and up to a 20-core GPU, which enables enhanced shader core and third-generation ray tracing for complex 3D design, VFX and game development.
And each GPU core has a neural accelerator so it delivers remarkable games and AI compute when compared to the previous Mac mini. You
Mac mini with M5 Pro can support up to 64 GB of unified memory.
Mac mini with M5 Pro delivers:
– Up to 8.5x faster LLM prompt processing performance5 in LM Studio when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 4x faster than M4 Pro.2
– Up to 4.5x faster rendering performance5 with ray tracing in Blender when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 1.4x faster than M4 Pro.2
– Up to 2.1x faster image processing5 in Affinity when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 1.5x faster than M4 Pro.2
MAC STUDIO WITH M5 MAX AND M5 ULTRA – From $4,299 (M5 MAX) and $9,499 (M5 ULTRA)
Mac Studio with M5 Max and the all-new M5 Ultra offers a stunning leap in AI performance with even faster graphics to meet the most demanding professional workflows.
It’s all still housed in the signature compact Apple design.
These new models offer up to 4.3x faster AI performance, up to 2x faster storage, and up to 1.8x faster graphics with up to 1.3x faster CPU speed.
The Mac Studio is aimed at creators, developers, AI researchers, data scientists, and any other professional user looking to push the boundaries of what’s possible.
With the powerful M5 Ultra Silicon Max Studio, it offers up to a 36-core CPU, up to an 80-core GPU, and a game-changing 512 GB of unified memory.
With this sort of power at your fingertips, Mac Studio with M5 Max will make it possible to run enormous LLMs entirely on device.
The new Mac Studios offer Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 for the very first time.
Thunderbolt 5 also provides stunning connectivity to take advantage of super-fast external storage.
Mac Studios can also be connected into a cluster that offers up to 3x faster performance for distributed AI inference.
Mac Studio with M5 Ultra enables:
– Up to 15.4x faster CopyCat ML training performance in Foundry Nuke when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 3.3x faster than M3 Ultra.
– Up to 9.8x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 4x faster than M3 Ultra.
– Up to 8.2x faster text-to-image performance when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 4.3x faster than M3 Ultra.
– Up to 4.7x faster scene rendering performance in Maxon Redshift when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 1.7x faster than M3 Ultra.
Mac Studio with M5 Max is built for users who expect power and performance but with a smaller footprint.
It is ideal for musicians, photographers, software engineers, and designers who are exploring 3D and motion graphics.
Maxx Studio with M5 Max has an 18-core CPU with six super cores and 12 performance cores, up to a 40-core GPU with neural accelerators to take it 50 per cent faster than the previous generation.
Mac Studio with M5 Max enables:
– Up to 10.7x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and 3.9x faster than M4 Max.
– Up to 7.4x faster text-to-image performance when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 3.5x faster than M4 Max.
– Up to 5.3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 3x faster than M4 Max.
– Up to 3.5x faster basecalling for DNA sequencing in Oxford Nanopore MinKNOW when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 1.9x faster than M4 Max.

articles.title: Pour fabriquer son incroyable iPhone en verre, Apple aurait trouvé une solution
articles.text:
L’année 2027 marquera les 20 ans de l’iPhone. Afin de célébrer cet anniversaire, Apple compte lancer un produit unique, soit un iPhone entièrement en verre. Ou presque. Certaines sources ont affirmé que l’entreprise à la pomme avait abandonné ce projet en raison de difficultés de production, mais le toujours très bien renseigné Mark Gurman a assuré le contraire : Apple prépare bien un « iPhone principalement en verre, incurvé et sans aucune découpe dans l’écran », selon le journaliste de Bloomberg. Ce verre incurvé envelopperait tous les côtés de l’appareil. Aujourd’hui, une nouvelle information vient confirmer les propos de Gurman.
Apple aurait mobilisé la chaîne de production de l’iPhone Air pour produire l’iPhone des 20 ans
Le leaker Fixed Focus Digital assure qu’Apple a modifié la chaîne de production de l’iPhone Air afin de l’adapter à la fabrication de l’iPhone des 20 ans. Pour rappel, l’iPhone Air est l’iPhone le plus fin d’Apple à ce jour, avec une épaisseur de 5,6 mm. Il présente un cadre en titane poli ainsi qu’un dos en verre.
Apple aurait ainsi mobilisé la chaîne de production de l’iPhone Air, tout en lui apportant quelques ajustements, afin de lancer prochainement la production de l’iPhone des 20 ans. Le procédé de fabrication et d’assemblage du verre serait ainsi similaire, mais certains équipements de production auraient été modifiés afin de confectionner des composants en verre plus arrondis.
Cela permettrait à Apple de réduire sensiblement ses coûts de fabrication. En effet, au lieu de créer de nouvelles chaînes de production, l’entreprise à la pomme en mobilise certaines déjà existantes. Mais surtout, le leaker assure que ces modifications apportées à la chaîne de production de l’iPhone Air ont permis à Apple d’améliorer considérablement la gestion de la dissipation thermique et le processus d’affinement de l’iPhone des 20 ans.
Il va falloir se montrer encore patient
Apple préparerait donc bel et bien un iPhone quasiment entièrement en verre. Cependant, cet appareil ne devrait pas être dévoilé avant l’automne 2027. Pour rappel, Apple présentera l’automne prochain l’iPhone 18 Pro, l’iPhone 18 Pro Max, l’iPhone Ultra et, normalement, les AirPods équipés de caméras, ainsi que sa nouvelle gamme d’appareils domotiques. Ensuite, au printemps 2027, nous devrions découvrir l’iPhone 18 standard, l’iPhone 18e et l’iPhone Air 2. Enfin, à l’automne 2027, Apple devrait clôturer les festivités avec l’iPhone des 20 ans. Il faudra donc encore patienter.

articles.title: Cuál es el valor en el mercado de la criptomoneda Bitcoin este día
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
PUBLICIDAD
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El costo de la criptomoneda de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 79054.35 dólares por unidad.
Esto quiere decir que la moneda digital anotó un cambio del 0.07% en el último día, así como una variación del 0.0% en los últimos 60 minutos.
PUBLICIDAD
Actualmente, bitcoin se encuentra en el lugar #1 de popularidad en el mercado digital. Cabe mencionar que el máximo histórico que ha alcanzado esta divisa digital es de 126.198 dólares por unidad.
Bitcoin alcanza un nuevo récord y lidera el auge en el mercado de las criptomonedas
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
PUBLICIDAD
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
PUBLICIDAD
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: Harry Potter (HBO Max) : Kit Harington remplace Nicholas Hoult dans le rôle de Gilderoy Lockhart
articles.text:
Harry Potter (HBO Max) : Kit Harington remplace Nicholas Hoult dans le rôle de Gilderoy Lockhart
Changement de programme à Poudlard, ce n'est finalement pas Nicholas Hoult qui incarnera le professeur Lockhart dans la saison 2 de la série Harry Potter, mais un visage bien connu des fans de Game of Thrones.
Retournement de situation en salle des profs ! Nicholas Hoult ne pourra finalement pas participer à la saison 2 de la série Harry Potter, faute de temps, alors c'est Kit Harington, le Jon Snow de Game of Thrones, qui va prendre sa place dans le show HBO Max.
De Westeros à Poudlard
On apprenait il y a une dizaine de jours que Nicholas Hoult incarnerait le professeur Lockhart dans la saison 2 de la série Harry Potter, mais HBO n'a finalement pas réussi à faire coexister le planning de tournage de sa série avec l'emploi du temps déjà chargé de l'acteur de Superman.
C'est donc Kit Harington, grand fan d'Harry Potter, qui a sauté sur l'occasion de reprendre le flambeau. Pour rappel, ce professeur de défense contre les forces du mal plus préoccupé par sa célébrité que par l'enseignement joue un rôle clé dans le second roman de la saga sur le sorciers à lunettes.
Harington connait d'ailleurs déjà très bien le rôle de Gilderoy Lockhart, autrefois campé par Kenneth Branagh dans l'adaptation cinématographique d'Harry Potter et la Chambre des Secrets.
L'acteur connu pour son rôle dans la série Game of Thrones a en effet prêté sa voix au personnage dans la version originale des livres audios Harry Potter récemment sortis sur Audible.
La série Harry Potter adapte les romans de J.K. Rowling sous la houlette de Francesca Gardiner (Succession), seule au poste de showrunner sur la première saison et accompagnée par Jon Brown (Veep) sur la saison 2.
Le tournage de cette saison 2 d'Harry Potter commencera cet automne et la diffusion de la première saison, intitulée Harry Potter à l'école des sorciers, est programmée pour Noël sur HBO Max.

articles.title: Draco, ce satellite suicidaire dont le seul but est d'aller se cramer pour de bon
articles.text:
L’histoire de la conquête spatiale, c’est soixante-dix ans de missions lancées vers les étoiles. Mais c’est aussi soixante-dix ans de retombées en tout genre. On évalue à environ 10 000 le nombre de satellites ou de morceaux de fusées qui sont retombés dans l’atmosphère, avant de finir en boule de feu, comme des étoiles filantes artificielles.
Si cela donne lieu à des scènes irréelles, comme cette désintégration d’un Starship filmée depuis un avion en plein vol, ces évènements restent plutôt mal connus. On ne sait pas très bien ce qui se passe dans les entrailles d’un satellite qui se brise avant de se consumer. C’est pour combler ce trou dans nos connaissances que la mission Draco a été pensée.
Draco, pour Destructive Reentry Assessment Container Object (comprendre : objet-conteneur pour l’évaluation des réentrées destructrices), a la taille d’une machine à laver et pèse entre 150 et 200 kg. Et, c’est tout. Il n’y a ni propulsion, ni système de navigation ou moyen de communication. Rien, ou presque. Draco sera pour l’essentiel passif.
Car ce programme, supervisé par l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA), n’est pas fait pour durer, au contraire. Il s’agit de le cramer littéralement. Dans le scénario qui a été retenu, il faudra transporter Draco aussi haut que possible dans l’atmosphère, puis le plonger à toute allure au-dessus d’une zone océanique, pour ne menacer personne.
Puisque l’idée est que Draco imite la fin de vie d’un satellite lambda qui se fait happer par l’atmosphère, il faut que sa chute soit représentative. Voilà pourquoi Draco n’aura pas de moteur. Il devra donc recourir à un lanceur pour être acheminé à 1 000 km d’altitude (la frontière de l’espace étant fixée par convention à 100 km).
Cette hauteur, qui le place au-dessus de la constellation Starlink ou de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS), doit offrir une séquence assez longue pour observer ce qui se passe. Et pour cela, Draco, bien que passif, ne sera pas tout à fait inerte. On parle de 200 capteurs et 4 caméras qui devront tout enregistrer.
La mission n’est pas sans un certain paradoxe : certes, il faut à la fois tout noter (température, pression environnante, vitesse de rentrée, contrainte sur la structure, angle, images et vidéos de la casse…), et donc préserver les enregistrements, tout en s’assurant de la destruction effective de Draco. Ou, plus précisément, d’une partie de la mission.
Un satellite jetable, une capsule survivaliste
En fait, il y a deux parties dans Draco : un satellite qui brûle comme les autres et, en son centre, une capsule increvable, capable d’encaisser l’enfer de la rentrée atmosphérique, pour ramener les données en toute sécurité sur Terre. C’est justement ce que rappelle l’ESA dans un point d’étape du 25 août 2026.
Et Stijn Lemmens, chef de projet Draco, a levé le voile sur certains aspects de la mission plutôt surprenants. Ainsi, la capsule, qui ne dépasse pas les 40 centimètres, est protégée par un bouclier thermique en liège portugais, testé à l’Institut von Karman (Belgique) en le bombardant de plasma pour imiter les conditions de rentrée.
Autre défi : la chorégraphie qui se déroulera dans le ciel. Il faut que la capsule puisse se détacher au bon moment, c’est-à-dire assez tard pour récolter un maximum de mesures, mais pas trop tard pour ne pas être non plus emportée dans la destruction générale. Car Draco devrait littéralement finir en toupie, à plus de cinq tours par seconde.
Tandis que le satellite va se mettre à tournoyer, la capsule devra parvenir à se stabiliser seule, sans aucun système de contrôle actif — et sa forme bien précise doit l’y aider. Vers 10 km d’altitude, elle doit larguer sa coque arrière et déployer un parachute. Viendra ensuite une chute d’environ 20 minutes, avant de finir sa course dans l’océan.
Durant cet intervalle, Draco doit pouvoir se connecter à un satellite situé en orbite et transférer entre 20 Mo et 1 Go de données.
La capsule, elle, n’est pas récupérée. Une fois son parachute déployé, elle transmet ses données puis termine sa course dans l’océan, sans être repêchée. Tout repose donc sur cette fenêtre de transmission : si les mesures ne remontent pas à temps vers un satellite relais, elles disparaissent avec l’engin. Embêtant.
Et pour ne pas se louper, l’Agence spatiale européenne prépare aussi une campagne d’observation depuis un avion, afin de recouper les données reçues et obtenir des compléments, cette fois depuis un point de vue plus bas. Draco emportera d’ailleurs des matériaux marqueurs qui produiront des étincelles vertes en se désagrégeant.
Une animation diffusée par l’ESA montre à quoi devrait ressembler cette rentrée vue de l’intérieur.
Pourquoi diable cramer un satellite exprès ?
Derrière une expérience qui plairait à n’importe qui adorant détruire des trucs, il y a une réelle réflexion sur un problème très concret : les orbites très encombrées.
Selon le rapport 2025 de l’ESA sur l’environnement spatial, environ 40 000 objets sont suivis autour de la Terre, dont à peine 11 000 satellites encore actifs ; le reste, ce sont des débris, et on estime à plus de 1,2 million ceux de plus d’un centimètre, trop petits pour être tracés mais capables de détruire un engin.
Même chose au sol : des satellites intacts rentrent déjà dans l’atmosphère plus de trois fois par jour en moyenne – une situation qui ne va pas aller en diminuant, avec le développement des méga-constellations. Plus on saura les faire brûler complètement, moins il restera de morceaux susceptibles de retomber sur la Terre, et d’être menaçants.
L’ESA vise le « zéro débris » pour ses missions d’ici 2030, avec le « design for demise » comme approche : concevoir dès le départ des engins qui se détruisent entièrement au retour. Il y a d’ailleurs une certaine ironie, qui a été pointée par Tim Flohrer, chef du Bureau des débris spatiaux. C’est Draco qui en théorie profiterait le plus des données que la mission va récolter.
Malgré son importance technique, Draco reste une expérience menée à petit budget (du moins à l’échelle de ce qui se fait dans le spatial), où une part de risque restera – une réalité que reconnait l’ESA. Cela se reflète aussi sur le contrat signé d’abord avec Deimos, à hauteur de 3 millions d’euros, avant d’être piloté aujourd’hui par l’industriel Indra.
Avant de simuler la chute finale d’un satellite, la capsule grandeur nature doit encore passer une série de tests d’ici à fin 2026, dont un largage de parachute depuis un ballon à 25 km d’altitude. Si toutes les étapes sont franchies sans anicroche, alors le lancement pourra avoir lieu en 2027, avec l’espoir de servir tous les autres satellites lancés après lui.

articles.title: AWS : Plus de 700 clés d'accès dans la nature, avec des droits admin
articles.text:
Le cabinet de sécurité Truffle Security a réexaminé plus de 10 000 clés d'accès AWS retrouvées en ligne entre 2022 et 2026. 88 % fonctionnaient encore lors du contrôle réalisé ce mois-ci.
Parmi les clés toujours actives, 768 appartiennent à des entreprises et donnent un contrôle total sur leurs comptes cloud. Certaines sont restées actives sans la moindre rotation pendant plus de cinq ans.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
Cinq ans d'ancienneté, aucune rotation : le profil type des clés compromises
L'entreprise de cybersécurité a passé au crible des dépôts Git, des images Docker, des registres de paquets, des journaux d'intégration continue et des jeux de données d'entraînement pour y repérer des identifiants AWS abandonnés. Nous rapportions en mai 2026 comment la CISA elle-même avait laissé des clés AWS actives sur un dépôt public pendant six mois avant qu'un chercheur français ne les repère. Pour Truffle Security ce type d'oubli est loin d'être une exception.
Sur 64 024 paires de clés recensées, une sur six est une clé "racine", le compte administrateur principal d'AWS, lequel ne peut donc être ni restreint ni limité par une politique de permissions. Les autres identifiants appartiennent à des utilisateurs IAM, les comptes secondaires créés à l'intérieur d'un compte AWS pour accorder des droits limités à chaque service ou employé. En croisant les coordonnées des comptes avec les noms d'utilisateur, Truffle Security a identifié 817 clés liées à des entreprises. Sur ce total, 526 sont des clés racine et 242 appartiennent à des utilisateurs IAM dotés de la politique "AdministratorAccess", soit 768 clés offrant un contrôle intégral d'un compte AWS d'entreprise. 130 clés racine supplémentaires concernent des comptes de gestion d'organisation, l'échelon qui administre tous les comptes d'une structure.
Hugging Face concentre à elle seule une bonne partie des clés retrouvées. La plateforme, où circulent des modèles et des jeux de données pour l'entraînement de l'IA, en héberge 8 482 encore actives dans 3 394 jeux de données publics. C'est d'ailleurs là qu'on y trouve le plus souvent des clés racines (17,9 % du total). Ces jeux de données reprennent souvent du code source public tel quel, identifiants compris.
Ces clés ne sont pas seulement nombreuses, elles sont aussi vieilles, et personne ne les renouvelle. La moitié des identifiants encore valides ont été créés il y a plus de cinq ans, et seuls 25 sur 2 903 dataient de moins d'un mois. La fuite est donc presque toujours ancienne. AWS applique de son côté une politique de quarantaine automatique, "AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine", dès qu'un identifiant exposé est détecté. Cela concerne 929 des 7 590 utilisateurs IAM actifs, mais 112 conservent une version de cette restriction qu'AWS n'applique plus depuis 2023, preuve que ces clés, signalées depuis au moins trois ans, fonctionnent pourtant toujours.
D'ailleurs, l'argent n'est pas surveillé de plus près. Sur les comptes pour lesquels le budget peut être consulté, seuls 9,5 % ont une alerte configurée, avec un plafond médian de 8 dollars. La dépense médiane est proche de zéro. Mais sur le seul mois de juillet, 50 comptes ont dépassé 1 000 dollars de facturation, 9 sont passés au-dessus de 10 000 dollars, soit 420 631 dollars cumulés sur l'échantillon analysé. Truffle Security recommande de supprimer les clés racine, de suivre l'ancienneté des clés IAM et de mettre en place une alerte de budget.

articles.title: Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, les configurations sur PC — Frandroid
articles.text:
Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy est un jeu d’action-aventure développé par le studio bordelais Asobo Studio et édité par Focus Entertainment. Il s’agit d’un préquel direct aux événements de A Plague Tale: Requiem. Le jeu sort le 27 août sur PC, PlayStation 5 et Xbox Series X/S (disponible Day One sur le Game Pass).
Le jeu se déroule en 1334, soit 15 ans avant Requiem. On y incarne Sophia, une contrebandière déjà vue dans les précédents volets. Ses aventures l’amènent sur l’île du Minotaure, où elle tente de comprendre ses liens avec l’histoire ancienne de la Prima Macula et de l’époque minoenne. Le gameplay promet d’être bien plus axé sur l’action et les combats que celui de Requiem, plus basé sur l’infiltration.
Si vous voulez monter un PC gamer de toutes pièces, rendez-vous sur notre guide des meilleures configurations PC à choisir.

Ces performances s’entendent sans technologie d’upscaling ou générations d’images (DLSS / FSR).
Quels composants choisir pour jouer à Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy sur votre PC gaming ?
Soyons honnêtes, ce n’est pas le meilleur moment pour changer les composants de votre tour. Pourquoi ? Parce que l’industrie fait face à une grosse crise de la mémoire. Elle frappe la mémoire vive (RAM), mais aussi la mémoire flash (NAND) qui équipe les SSD. Une véritable pénurie est en cours, qui ne fait que s’aggraver : résultat, les prix de ces composants explosent.
Gaming ou études, pourquoi choisir ? Équipement tech, PC et écrans : profitez de jusqu’à -40 % pour la rentrée chez PcComponentes ! Livraison offerte dès 50 € et garantie remplacement 24 h jusqu’au 12 septembre.

Monter sa tour PC ou mettre à niveau ses composants n’est pas à la portée de toutes les bourses. Il existe une solution simplissime et bien moins chère : le cloud gaming.

articles.title: Linux Foundation to Govern TRACE, an Open Standard for AI Runtime Attestation
articles.text:
The Linux Foundation said Tuesday it will take on governance of TRACE (Trust, Runtime Attestation and Compliance Evidence), a new open specification for producing verifiable evidence of how AI agents and other confidential workloads run.
Contributed by confidential computing vendor OPAQUE, the specification was developed jointly with AMD, Intel, Microsoft, and the Technology Innovation Institute (TII).
TRACE creates a hardware-backed, cryptographically verifiable record that ties together the runtime environment, the software executed, the policies applied, the classification of any data involved, and which tools an AI agent invoked.
The resulting artifact is designed to be portable across different cloud providers, confidential computing platforms, and sovereign infrastructure.
The push for a common standard comes as organizations move AI agents beyond isolated experiments into production environments that handle sensitive data and span multiple systems, a shift OPAQUE said increases the need for evidence that can be independently verified.
The company highlighted the recent incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and hacked Hugging Face. Similar incidents were also reported by Meta and Anthropic.
Rather than building a new verification framework from scratch, TRACE combines a set of existing, established standards — RATS, EAT, SLSA, SCITT, SPIFFE and EAR — into a single evidence layer intended to work across enterprise, cloud and sovereign AI deployments.
“TRACE provides the open source community with a unified, hardware-attested specification for compliance and security evidence. By hosting TRACE under neutral governance, we are ensuring trust in AI remains open, portable and verifiable across any infrastructure,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation.
AMD senior fellow Mahesh Wagh said the company’s SEV technology provides the silicon-level protection for data and models while they’re in use, with TRACE turning that protection into evidence.
Intel’s Anand Pashupathy noted that hardware-based attestation and confidential computing give organizations cryptographic evidence of an agent’s identity, its authorized actions, and confirmation that governance policies are enforced.
TRACE’s reference library has recorded roughly 135,000 downloads on PyPI within ten weeks of its initial introduction at the Confidential Computing Summit in June 2026. The open specification, technical documentation, and reference implementations are available at trace.agentrust-io.com and on GitHub.

articles.title: Continuous Delivery for Foundational Platforms
articles.text:
Transcript
Ian Nowland: My name is Ian Nowland. I'm co-founder of Junction Labs. A little bit about my background as it applies to the talk. I was at Amazon 10 years, AWS 8 years, 2008 - 2016, mostly on EC2. EC2 was basically a stack of platforms that I got to learn a lot from. I left there in 2016, I moved to New York. I had a 50-person compute platform team at a FinTech, that's where I met Camille, my co-author. Then I jumped to Datadog, pre-IPO, and just saw the rocket ship there, where again, I just saw these platform teams just challenged by the assumptions that what they should be doing is what all the product teams were doing. I wrote the book, of course. I'm now co-founder of a startup called Junction Labs.
Terminology
I want to start just with a couple of definitions. There's this foundational platform, which is a little bit of a weasel, and I just want to say why I have that. To me, the big difference between a foundational platform and a non-foundational platform is just if you break, does the business go down? That's different to maybe a developer experience platform you deploy, where some engineers are very frustrated with you, but very different to, we're actually no longer making trades, if we're a financial company. If we're an observability company, we're no longer ingesting data. I think it just changes the way that you build platforms. That's the purpose of the talk. Another definition, I actually did not understand this before I started preparing this talk, and I actually don't think it matters too much. If you go back, I think about 5 to 10 years ago, there's one CD, it's a deployment versus delivery.
There's this idea that deployment is fully automated all the way to production. I haven't seen much of that in my career. I don't want to say it doesn't exist at all. Then there's continuous delivery, which is the much more, ok, you get through CI and then a human presses a button, and everything is perfectly automated on either side. I do think for application teams, product teams, that's possible. I think it's platform teams' jobs to make that possible. It's much harder for platform teams itself. A lot of this talk is why that is and what you should do about it.
Outline
My outline is first answering why a typical CD doesn't work for foundational platforms. Then I'll go back, like a lot of what I think I learned works and doesn't work, was just seeing EC2, and it was both of them. We tried a lot of things that should have worked, and they just didn't work for a foundational platform. Then I tried to apply those rules at Datadog and got some more lessons. Then finally just wrapping it up.
1. Why Typical CD Doesn't Work for Foundational Platforms
Why a typical CD doesn't work for foundational platforms. I want to start with, again, you're on a platform team. Highest latency between the service of EC2 and EBS, on racks with the worst packet loss. Packet loss was just other customers on the rack doing things. The numbers are tight, like 1 in 100,000, but it was enough packet loss to start spiking it. Then the TCP tunings actually made things worse. To this again, it just comes back to when you have a really large surface area of complexity that you're abstracting over to, tiny little things that are impossible to test against are going to make things worse. The big thing with this one, we did have a metric that we actually weren't watching at the time in our own little data plane software. That's fine. If we'd been watching this one metric, we would have seen this very quickly before we'd even run out to 10% of the fleet and pulled it back.
What didn't work was big broad customer facing SLOs getting into these big broad error budgets. Systems are way too complex. I can tell you each of my teams had between 20 and probably by the end close to 50, they have a dashboard with all these graphs. They weren't looking at it constantly, but they were looking at it constantly around a deployment. Like, I know I went out to 5% of the fleet, did anything just spike? It was very hard to automate it. We did get better over time, worked out how to automate this graph watching. What we needed, especially early on to manage risk was just people looking at the graphs. The takeaway is just roll out slowly and observe deeply.
Putting it all together, this is just a nice pipeline view. Up to the pre-CI stuff, prod canaries first, where your synthetic tests are, go there first. That's the way you discover actually in production, do you work against your dependencies? Small region, something where your customers have lower standards is the ideal, I think, for a general platform. Deploy to a subset of your largest, riskiest AZ early. Then slow rollout hours per AZ. At Datadog we were faster than this, but we did end up using a very similar pipeline.
3. 2019 - 2023 Datadog: Scaling Safe Testing in Production in a CI/CD Culture
Next thing, this is Datadog, 2019 to 2023. This is me taking what I learned at Amazon, coming in as a VP and trying to help a platform team that was having problems. Datadog was 350 engineers. My org was initially 50, within about a year was about a third of this. The big thing with Datadog is we were hiring aggressively. The cultural issues were a big problem. Compared to EC2 we weren't big, but we weren't tiny. We had about 10,000 VMs in two regions. Product teams like Datadog was very proud of its success versus things like CloudWatch. They did have a great product culture. Things like feature flags, things like being able to get something in front of a customer against their real production data and getting feedback from that was a big part of how Datadog grew as fast as it did. That was the product team.
The platform teams were forced to keep up. That was failing as things were getting bigger and bigger. Feature flag-heavy culture, good product. Datadog at the time was acceptably flaky. The customers were customers like Airbnb and Shopify. Generally, with observability, it's not the end of the world if it goes down for startups. As companies get bigger and bigger and it blocks your deployments, it becomes an important thing. That was happening at Datadog. You had these enterprise customers come in with much higher standards about outages. The problem that I had was how to apply safe, progressive deployment without slowing the customer culture.
Introduction to practices. What didn't work was me as platform SVP dictating what worked at his last company. I say this through experience, because Camille, my co-author, based on our time together at Two Sigma, the FinTech, sent me these cups. These are literally cups she sent me. They say at Amazon We. Camille was suggesting I use that phrase a little bit too often. What you learn is processes dictated by an SVP will be done poorly because people don't understand why they're doing it. They're only doing it because someone up on top is yelling at them to do them. Processes done badly are worse than no processes. Generally, like you have to find a way to motivate people within a culture to start doing better than you. What worked for me was to get very regular. I ended up doing an Amazon thing. We did weekly post-mortem reviews.
I made sure I attended. I didn't really yell like Charlie Bell, but I did make sure my voice was heard at those meetings about making sure the team who was just impacted, they were where I was going to introduce the best practices. I didn't go broad with it. It was like starting with the effective teams, find the champions. That's how I managed to scale it. To introduce practices, start small, and expand.
Deployment planning. Now this is on the flip side though. You start doing this, you start seeing success, but you still see particularly when you're hiring fast and then also acquiring that every team almost has to get bitten before they want to start doing the better thing. Of course, that's really bad when you're launching product after product after product, because customers get very frustrated. Deployment planning, when I talked about it earlier, actually making people plan out the deployments. This ended up being product teams as well as the platform team. What didn't work was just saying, here's some best practices. Go talk to the champions, and then go, let you do what you want. What happened was we had one bad outage, but we also just had this trend of increasing number of outages. Rapid hiring plus acquisitions, no consistent norms. Product mindset, again, it's a good thing, but it does tend to mean that reliability is just reactive to current trends.
You see these in the product managers. They don't give a shit about reliability until you have an outage. They're like, why don't you do better, engineers? It's like you're yelling at us to do faster. What did work was after a major outage, my manager, Alexis, and the CTO and myself, I mandated phased deploys. I didn't want to enforce it on everyone without getting some amount of buy-in. I created a group of staff engineers to standardize and we rolled it out to their orgs. This is basically the same takeaway as earlier, if you touch prod manually, it needs review. It's a fact of life for platforms. Feature flags. What didn't work well for us was feature flags. The code was just getting way too complex. The blast radius was too big. Infra rollouts were slow. What did work is this technique of sandboxes and shadow deployments.
I hadn't seen this used this much before, but parts of data were really good at this. A lot of my job was just making sure I was advocated to a larger role. It's basically, find a way to iterate on code without affecting customers. I wanted to do a picture, like this is a very simplified picture of Datadog. This is before doing any shadow deployments. What you see is two things here. The first thing is your data engineering team, this is why they love Kafka. Kafka is this really nice thing because you can just like put this new code in production and make sure it doesn't affect anything downstream, pull from Kafka, and test it against real data. That's a great thing. What you see is this combination with sandboxing on the right. If you can pass through headers saying that you're basically a test account, now they can get down to where they are in the stack and actually test against the storage code as well. You see on the left, the async with Kafka, on the right, the synchronous. The technique is called sandboxing.
Finally, deployment tools. I had the deployment tool team rolling up to me for almost the complete time I was at Datadog. There was this strong drive, like, we just need one great CD tool for all teams. It just never worked. It was just one of those things that, especially as a leader, they're like, I couldn't keep throwing engineers trying to build this very bespoke, but great deployment tool. What was happening was the platform teams, because they had all that complexity, because of the statefulness we talked about earlier, they just needed complex features that the app teams didn't. It didn't make any sense for them to prioritize the platform teams ahead of the app teams, because the app teams were the ones we wanted to move faster. We wanted them to use the proper CD. It did work with the platform teams hiring their own SREs, build platform-specific automation. This is something where it's counter maybe to the Amazon list. It's a place where we just needed teams building automation. Platform teams often need to invest more in automation.
4. Core Takeaways
Core takeaways. As I said, I'm a strong believer in this. I know it's painful. I just haven't seen anything else work for foundational platforms at scale. Prioritize synthetic monitoring. Again, it's the biggest thing, having left AWS that I saw missing in the teams that I inherited. Find a way to iterate on code in prod without affecting customers. Look if feature flags work for you and it's great. Otherwise look at some other techniques. Time finds problems, people fix them. This, I think, is the core thing we know about platforms. It's a nice thing to send Marc's blog post to people when they're critiquing why you were so slow. Roll out slowly and observe deeply. Yes, platform teams, we often need to just do this or everything that I've said above, ourselves. We can't rely on the company platform because we're one and there's a thousand other teams who want something else. This is the final summary, which is just for foundational platforms, continuous delivery requires safe progressive deployments.
Questions and Answers
Participant 1: Can you provide your definition of synthetic monitoring?
Ian Nowland: What it looked like at Amazon was something that called the APIs from the top as if it was a customer focused on one vertical segment of functionality. It wasn't like the dumb just hit a website with HTTP. It was complete workflows. Probably the easiest one to answer was when I was on Elastic MapReduce, the synthetic monitoring I built there would actually start a cluster, run some jobs on the cluster, terminate the cluster. I think of it as a mini user simulation for a vertical, but using the API is just like a gut. I think that's one of the key things. I talk about it in the book. It really forces your internal engineering team to go through the pain. Like if you're flaky, then your customers are going to experience this as well. It's end-to-end workflows, pretending you're a customer, essentially.

articles.title: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 with GB205 Appears in Third-Party AIB Design
articles.text:
Tuesday, August 25th 2026
	
		
	
	
	
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 with GB205 Appears in Third-Party AIB Design
NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 5060 mid-range graphics card is officially based on the GB206 GPU die SKU, equipped with 3,840 CUDA cores, 120 TMUs, 48 ROPs, and a total of 8 GB of GDDR7 memory running on a 128-bit bus. This is the standard configuration, which is supposed to be the same across every RTX 5060 GPU you buy from any of NVIDIA's add-in board partners. However, a review of the ASUS DUAL GeForce RTX 5060 OC D7 8 GB by Intek & Company, Quasar Zone revealed that the GPU die inside this graphics card is actually a GB205-200-KB-A1 GPU die SKU. This die is usually found in NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 5070, RTX 5070 Ti Mobile, and RTX PRO 3000 "Blackwell" mobile graphics cards.
When NVIDIA does these GPU SKU crossovers, it usually comes down to binning. Sometimes, GPUs of a lower bin do not meet all the parametric yields, meaning not all CUDA cores are functional. In such cases, the company can repurpose these GPUs as a lower-tier design, as is the case with the RTX 5060. Instead of this SKU going into an RTX 5070 and lacking CUDA cores, ROPs, or TMUs, it is cut down to RTX 5060 specs and used as an RTX 5060 base. No performance difference should be present.In testing by Quasar Zone, the GB205-based RTX 5060 performs relatively the same, with some exceptions where performance is higher. This is likely due to the out-of-the-box overclocking applied to this model.

articles.title: Mac Mini mit M6 vorgestellt: Das Gehäuse bleibt klein, der Preis nicht
articles.text:
Mac Mini mit M6 vorgestellt: Das Gehäuse bleibt klein – der Preis nicht
Apple aktualisiert seine populären Desktop-Computer Mac Mini und Mac Studio mit stärkeren Chips. Die Kleincomputer wurden in den vergangenen Jahren zu Bestsellern für den iPhone-Konzern, insbesondere wenn es um lokale Anwendungen mit künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) geht.
Mit den neuen Chipsystemen der hauseigenen M-Reihe sollen sich die aufgefrischten Modelle noch besser für solche KI-Zwecke eignen.
Viel mehr Leistung, höhere Preise
Der Mac Mini, der bisher mit M4- und M4-Pro-Chips angeboten wurde, wird auf M6 und M5 Pro aufgerüstet. Schon mit dem M6-Chip soll der Mac Mini eine bis zu viermal schnellere KI-Leistung bieten als die Vorgängergeneration. Die Speicherchips können die Daten laut Apple doppelt so schnell verarbeiten.
Der Startpreis beim Mac Mini steigt von bisher 949 auf 1.049 Euro. Apple hat wie andere Hardware-Hersteller damit zu kämpfen, dass sich Speicherchips wegen des hohen Bedarfs für KI-Rechenzentren drastisch verteuert haben. In den vergangenen Monaten gab es wegen der schwierigen Chip-Verfügbarkeit Lieferengpässe bei einigen Geräten der Firma.
Neuer, leistungsstärkster Apple-Chip
Den Mac Studio frischt Apple mit dem M5-Max-Chip auf – und verwendet auch erstmals das neue Chipsystem M5 Ultra, das bisher leistungsstärkste des Konzerns. Für den Ultra-Chip werden zwei Max-Halbleiter verbunden. Mit bis zu 36 Hauptprozessor-Kernen und bis zu 80 Grafikkernen soll er unter anderem das lokale Training von KI-Modellen mit größeren Datensätzen ermöglichen. Der Startpreis beim Mac Studio mit Max-Chip bleibt mit 2.999 Euro unverändert.
Beim Mac Mini ist es das erste Hardware-Update seit fast zwei Jahren, der Mac Studio wurde zuletzt im Frühjahr 2025 aktualisiert.

articles.title: Tesla just killed Solar Roof after years of complaints and price hikes
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Tesla has stopped taking orders for Solar Roof, ending its push to sell solar shingles as an alternative to conventional rooftop panels. The decision reflects the high costs and installation challenges that kept the solar-shingle product from becoming commercially viable.
The company told its certified third-party installers that Solar Roof is no longer available for new projects. Tesla will continue selling standard solar panels and home battery systems instead. Its former Solar Roof web address now sends visitors to the company's solar-panel page.
The move follows years of high costs, difficult installations, and customer complaints. Two sources close to the program told Electrek that Tesla determined the product was not financially viable.
Solar Roof used glass tiles designed to generate electricity while serving as roofing material. That made the system more complicated than standard solar arrays, which are mounted above an existing roof. Tesla needed specialized equipment to make the tiles, and installation often required more customized work.
The added expense appears to have been a central problem. Solar Roof was positioned as a cleaner-looking option for homeowners who did not want visible solar panels, but demand was not enough to support the product's manufacturing costs.
Owners also reported problems after installation. Some customers faced long waits for repairs and high service costs. Others raised concerns about temperature management, possibly because the integrated tiles did not provide the same airflow as conventional panels mounted on racks above a roof.
Tesla also faced disputes over Solar Roof pricing. Some customers said Tesla increased project quotes substantially after contracts were signed, sometimes by as much as 100%. Those complaints led to a class-action lawsuit that Tesla settled in 2023.
Tesla has not said it will stop supporting homes that already have Solar Roof systems. Existing owners should remain covered under warranty, though the end of new sales means the company will no longer be adding to the product's customer base.
The company's shift puts more focus on conventional rooftop panels and battery storage, including the Powerwall. Those products use established supply chains and installation methods and do not require replacing a home's roof with specialized photovoltaic tiles.
Tesla's decision does not end the market for solar shingles. GAF and Merlin Solar still offer products designed to generate power as part of a roof. But Tesla's exit removes a high-profile player from a category that has struggled to move beyond a relatively small share of the residential solar market.

articles.title: Is Philips Hue about to do the unthinkable? It looks like it's about to launch a way to integrate Nanoleaf's awesome light panels to the Hue app
articles.text:
Philips Hue and Nanoleaf could soon reveal an unlikely tie-in — leaked adapter promises to bring Nanoleaf LED modules to your Hue app
Two become one
- Philips Hue could be launching a light module that lets you connect your Nanoleaf Shapes to the Hue app
- You'll be able to integrate Nanoleaf lights into your Hue schedules and automations
- It's not Matter-over-Thread, but you might be able to use a Hue Bridge for third-party connectivity
We’re just one week from IFA 2026, and we already have our ears to the ground for all the pre-event announcements and rumors — and this latest Philips Hue leak is bound to make Nanoleaf users very happy.
As spotted by the outlet Smartlights, Philips is reportedly launching the Hue Wall Light Module next week, meaning that users will be able to integrate their Nanoleaf lights into the Philips Hue ecosystem — which would be a huge win, especially since Nanoleaf is an affordable alternative to the Philips Hue range of best smart lights.
The Hue Wall Light Module is said to support the Nanoleaf Shapes LED panels, including Mini Triangles, Triangles, and Hexagons, while older panels (formerly known as Aurora) won’t be supported. Philips’ new module is also expected to be announced on September 3, and will go on sale for 39.99 euros, with international prices expected to follow.
Essentially, the rumored Hue module is a small white adapter around 8cm that you can plug directly into the connectors in your Nanoleaf panels, allowing you to integrate up to 100 Nanoleaf Shapes panels into your Hue system. That said, the Hue Wall Light Module shouldn’t be confused with the existing Philips Hue Wall Switch Module, which is installed behind a standard wall switch.
Once your Nanoleaf panels are connected via Philips’ new module, you’ll be able to include them in automations, Hue scenes, and schedules in the Hue app — but whether Nanoleaf’s flagship lighting tools will be carried over is unclear.
Similar to Philips Hue, Nanoleaf offers customizable color scenes and animations, but as far as the leaks go, the product images show the Nanoleaf integration working primarily with Hue scenes and effects. The leak shows at least five points in the color selection wheel, suggesting that there’ll be some kind of multicolor control function regardless, but we’ll have to see how this will work after the launch.
The other catch is that the Philips Hue Wall Light Module isn’t Matter-over-Thread, which, considering Nanoleaf’s devices are mainly Thread- and Matter-supported, is a bit of a departure. Instead, the module uses Zigbee and Bluetooth, the main connectivity protocols Philips has used for some time.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
That said, using a Hue Bridge allows you to connect Philips Hue devices that are non-Matter to hubs such as the Apple HomePod, which is helpful if you use the best smart speakers to control your home lighting system — though we’ll have to wait and see how the new Philips Hue module handles third-party connectivity once it’s launched.
Despite these gray areas, the Nanoleaf-Hue integration is an unexpected yet possibly beneficial upgrade. When it comes to smart lighting brands, their respective devices tend to keep you locked into one ecosystem or the other, so having a simple but effective connectivity tool would give users much more flexibility.

articles.title: Heelr launches marketplace for identity-verified cybersecurity experts - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Heelr launches marketplace for identity-verified cybersecurity experts
Luxembourg-based Heelr today launched a business-to-business platform that connects organizations with identity-verified cybersecurity professionals for contract and project work.
Companies can hire through the new platform for penetration testing, compliance preparation and virtual chief information security officer work. Rates advertised on the site for sample providers run from $145 to $250 an hour.
Heelr is aiming at buyers who have no security function of their own to call on. That covers founders, operations staff and information technology managers who end up owning security questions by default.
Providers have to clear an identity check before they can accept paid work, and Heelr validates their credentials separately. Engagements are broken into milestone payments. The company says that structure gives both sides more confidence about getting what they agreed to.
Compliance deadlines drive much of the demand. A customer security questionnaire, an ISO 27001 audit or a penetration test booked ahead of a product launch all arrive with a date attached, and the European Union’s NIS2 and DORA rules have added more of them. Few smaller companies keep a full-time security team on hand to absorb that work.
Heelr also pointed to artificial intelligence as a factor in the demand. Small teams now build and ship products at a pace that would have needed a much larger engineering group a few years ago. Few of those teams include a security engineer.
Security services are the largest single line item in corporate security budgets. Gartner Inc. expects worldwide spending on them to reach $86.1 billion in 2026, a bit more than 40% of all cybersecurity spending.
Laurent Halimi, chief executive of Heelr and its parent company Cyberr SA, said the security industry has changed enormously over the past decade while the way companies buy security expertise has barely moved. Buyers still fall back on “referrals, email chains and manual contracting” when they need an outside specialist, he said. Halimi added that general-purpose freelancer sites offer little assurance that a cybersecurity professional has the expertise claimed, “or that they are even who they say they are.”
Heelr does not start empty. Its providers come out of Cyberr, the professional network for cybersecurity workers that Cyberr SA also runs. Members there keep verified credential listings and look for work.
The Cyberr platform launched in March 2024, after Nexten.io merged with the U.K. recruitment firm Elite. Halimi has run the combined business out of Luxembourg since then. Last year the company picked up the French cybersecurity community CyberTee.
The provider side is open too. Independent consultants can list themselves on the platform. Boutique security firms can as well.
The platform is generally available starting today.

articles.title: Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 now available for pre-order in Canada
articles.text:
Asus announced when its latest gaming handheld, the ROG Xbox Ally X20, will be available ahead of Gamescom on Aug. 25. Moreover, we finally learned the price — an eye-watering $1,899 in Canada.
And if for some reason you wanted to spend even more money, Asus also has a bundle with the Ally X20 and the ROG Xreal R1 Edition 20 augmented reality (AR) glasses.
The Xbox Ally X20 sports a translucent black chassis with gold-accented internals and debuts ROG’s Nebula HDR OLED display. The screen measures in at 7.4 inches with a 1080p resolution and up to a 120Hz refresh rate.
Other specs include an AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme processor, 24GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, and an 80Wh battery. Those are very similar specs to the ROG Xbox Ally X, with the big difference being the larger OLED display.
Meanwhile, the ROG Xreal R1 Edition 20 glasses sport 0.55-inch Sony Micro OLED displays with a per-eye resolution of 1920×1080 pixels and a 120Hz refresh rate, or 240Hz with frame boost. The glasses also feature Bose speakers and a mic with noise cancellation.
As mentioned up top, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 on its own costs $1,899 in Canada, while the bundle with the AR glasses jumps up to $3,499. Notably, that makes it quite a bit more expensive than the Xbox Ally X at $1,499, and even more than the regular Xbox Ally at $799.
While MobileSyrup liked both the Xbox Ally models when they launched last year, we also cited the high price as an issue. The Xbox Ally X20 costs even more without adding a ton to the formula, so I’m not sure it’s worth the money.
ROG Xbox Ally Canadian review: Great handheld that costs too much
Still, if you want to buy one, the standalone Xbox Ally X20 will be available for pre-order starting today at Best Buy, and on Sept. 24 at the Asus Store, while the bundle with the ROG Xreal R1 Edition 20 AR glasses will be available for pre-order starting Sept. 24. Both begin shipping on October 15.

articles.title: Dolly Parton, la reina de la música country, ha muerto a los 80 años
articles.text:
Dolly Parton, considerada la reina del country y un ícono tanto de la música, como del cine y la TV, ha muerto a los 80 años. La noticia de su fallecimiento fue dada a conocer a través de sus redes sociales oficiales, por intermedio de un vídeo protagonizado por Bryan Seaver, su sobrino.
Si bien no se ha especificado la causa de su muerte, Dolly Parton llevaba algún tiempo acarreando problemas de salud. Estos la habían alejado de los escenarios en la parte final de su vida, impidiendo que concretara los shows de residencia en Las Vegas que tenía programados para septiembre próximo.
"El legado de Dolly Parton es de amor, compasión y resiliencia. Con una carrera de siete décadas, inspiró a múltiples generaciones de artistas y fans con su música y un compromiso inquebrantable para hacer del mundo un lugar mejor. Sus canciones seguirán resonando en personas de todas las edades, y su labor filantrópica tendrá un impacto duradero", publicó su familia.
"Dolly me llamó y me dijo que quería descansar en una hermosa cama de algodón suave porque, después de toda una vida llevando pesados diamantes de imitación, finalmente se merecía estar cómoda y descansar un poco", dijo Seaver en el anuncio de su fallecimiento.
Dolly Parton, un ícono de la música, el cine y la TV
Dolly Parton comenzó su carrera como cantante cuando todavía era una niña. Sin embargo, el éxito no le llegó de inmediato; de hecho, comenzó a ganar notoriedad en la industria como compositora de canciones para otros artistas. Su explosión como cantante se dio tras el lanzamiento de Hello, I'm Dolly, su primer disco de música country, en 1967.
A partir de allí, Dolly Parton se convirtió en figura del género, lo que luego le valió el mote de "reina de la música country". No obstante, hacia finales de los años setenta redobló sus esfuerzos para expandir su llegada a más personas, rompiendo los confines del country para codearse con figuras de otros géneros como pop, soul, rock y americana, entre otros.
En paralelo, Dolly Parton desarrolló una interesante carrera en el cine y la televisión. Su trabajo más famoso como actriz seguramente sea 9 to 5, de 1980, película para la cual compuso la canción homónima que se convirtió en clásico. Así cosechó la primera de sus dos nominaciones a los Premios Oscar por Mejor canción original. Si bien no pudo ganar el prestigioso galardón por sus composiciones, sí recibió el Premio Humanitario Jean Hersholt que otorga la Academia en 2025.
A lo largo de su carrera, Dolly Parton se convirtió en una figura frecuente de los principales galardones de la industria del entretenimiento. Fue ganadora de múltiples Premios Grammy y Emmy, y también cosechó nominaciones a los Globo de Oro y a los Premios Tony. En 2022, en tanto, se la introdujo al Salón de la Fama del Rock and Roll.
Fuera de la música y la actuación, Dolly Parton tuvo una importante faceta como empresaria. Uno de sus emprendimientos más rutilantes fue Dollywood, un parque de atracciones en Tennessee que atrae a millones de visitantes cada año.
Dolly Parton también ha sido especialmente reconocida por sus aportes filantrópicos. Fue una férrea defensora de la comunidad LGBTQ+ durante toda su carrera; asimismo, realizó importantes donaciones para financiar estudios médicos y farmacológicos. Uno de los más recordados fue durante durante la pandemia de la COVID-19, cuando impulsó el desarrollo de vacunas y su aplicación.

articles.title: Decades-long Linux ownership dispute effectively dead after Xinuos appeal rejected — US Court of Appeals halts the legal wrangling over IBM’s and Red Hat’s use of Project Monterey UNIX code
articles.text:
Decades-long Linux ownership dispute effectively dead after Xinuos appeal rejected — US Court of Appeals halts the legal wrangling over IBM’s and Red Hat’s use of Project Monterey UNIX code
Xinuos plans to petition for a full‑bench rehearing of its case, but this kind of request has only a 0.03% success rate according to IBM’s lawyers.
A decades-long dispute over the ownership of Linux looks like it is over. Earlier this month, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit rejected Xinuos’ continued claims that IBM and Red Hat improperly contributed jointly‑developed Project Monterey UNIX code to Linux, reports The Register. Despite this deathly blow to its chances of extracting potential damages from IBM and Red Hat, and oodles of Linux royalties and licensing fees, Xinuos intends to seek a full‑bench rehearing. This appeal is a very long shot for Xinuos, with only 0.03% of such hearings granted, according to IBM’s legal representatives in the dispute.
This is a complicated case that spans decades. So, to make sense of what has happened over the years, we’ve constructed a timeline of key events, spanning from way back in 1998 to the present day.
- 1998 Project Monterey. IBM partnered with a firm called Santa Cruz Operation (SCO), Intel, and Sequent to build a unified UNIX running on multiple processor architectures. SCO’s contribution was largely related to Intel x86 code.
- 1998-2001. Linux enjoyed rapid growth, so the importance of Project Monterey waned. IBM saw the shifting sands and moved its focus to Linux.
- Early 2000s. SCO first complained that IBM contributed jointly‑developed UNIX code to Linux without having proper rights to do so. Litigation began.
- 2003. SCO’s first major lawsuit was filed against IBM. It asked for billions of dollars due to the aforementioned complaint of IBM’s unauthorized use of UNIX code in Linux.
- 2011. Xinuos bought SCO’s UNIX business and IP.
- 2021. The SCO heir settled with IBM for $14.25 million. That’s a far smaller sum than it asked for in 2003, which kind of reflects SCO’s failure to produce convincing legal evidence.
- 2021. Xinuos sued IBM and Red Hat, claiming that IBM knowingly breached its non‑exclusive license by contributing Monterey code to Linux.
- 2022-2025. Xinuos argued that IBM’s actions amounted to licensing violations, but the U.S. District Court (SDNY) rejected this claim.
- August 10, 2026. Xinuos’ appeals are rejected. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled that the case was too old to relitigate, and Xinuos framed it as licensing but was really arguing ownership, which is time‑barred. Thus the District Court dismissal stood.
- Now, August 2026. Xinuos has announced that it will petition for a full‑bench rehearing of its case. However, this is a long shot with a 0.03% chance of a rehearing being granted. According to IBM’s defense law firm.
While Xinuos looks like it has run out of road on its Linux code ownership claims, that’s probably good for the computing community. IBM, Red Hat, and the open-source world can probably now rest a little easier, with the shadow cast in 2003 now nearly entirely removed. Lingering uncertainty over Linux’s legitimacy is evaporating with the Second Circuit’s affirmation that the case is time-barred, and rather hollow, legally.
Other companies contributing code to open source projects can also rest a little easier as this distracting, resource-draining litigation grinds to a halt. Success for Xinuous may have also meant billions of Linux devices facing licensing uncertainty, maker settlements, audits, and/or forced software rewrites.
